newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: UN Council endorses Central Africa peacekeepers.
newsitem.headline: UN Council endorses Central Africa peacekeepers.

text.p: The U.N. Security Council on Wednesday endorsed an African peacekeeping operation in the Central African Republic and authorised the use of force in monitoring accords aimed at ending army mutinies.
A resolution adopted unanimously by the 15-member body approved the force of about 1,000 soldiers from six countries to monitor the accords "in a neutral and impartial way."
The troops -- from Burkina Faso, Chad, Gabon, Mali, Senegal and Togo with French logistical experts -- also are authorised to use force in self-defence for three months.

To this end, the document invoked Chapter 7 of the U.N. Charter that allows the use of force following June attacks against the peacekeepers. This section of the resolution will be reviewed after three months, thereby giving the council some role in monitoring the operation.

The endorsement by the council gives the troops international legitimacy but does not finance them as a U.N. peacekeeping force. "Expenses and logistical support will be born on a voluntary basis," the resolution said.

France, as part of its new policy to withdraw many of its troops from Africa, plans to pull most of its 1,400 soldiers out of the Central African Republic. But it is supplying some 100 logistics experts for the African force, diplomats said.
The force is to disarm rebels and help maintain security after army mutinies a year ago turned into a campaign to oust President Ange-Felix Patasse, who was elected in 1993.

U.S. Ambassador Bill Richardson said the force was an "important milestone in the development of an indigenous African peacekeeping capability," which the United States, France and Britain and others are trying to promote.

The new peacekeeping operation began in February and is called MISAB, the Inter-African Mission to Monitor the Bangui Accords. It was formed after January accords were drawn up in Bangui, the capital, in an effort to stop the mutinies.

Mali's respected former military leader, Amadou Toumani Toure, brokered the deal but the mutinies continued sporadically. He moved in again to re-estabish the peace accords after weeklong clashes broke out again in June between army dissidents and the African peacekeepers.

The formal request for council authorisation came from Patasse as well as Gabon's President Omar Bongo, whose country is leading the force. It was strongly supported in the council by African members Kenya, Guinea-Bissau and Egypt.
France has a defence pact with its former colony, whose main source of wealth is diamonds and where self-proclaimed Emperor Jean-Bedel Bokassa ruled from 1966 to 1979.
